added_claim_errors: "risks forfeiting roughly $1,220–$1,240": the $1,240 end uses the $660 cap that applies to the 2025 plan year, not this 2026 year, so the range muddles the figure (should be $1,220 at the IRS maximum)
"Unused carryover still expires later": imprecise; carryover money can itself be carried again under a plan's cap, so this is loosely stated
Cites a payroll.org blog for the 2026 limits: a checkable link, but not the primary IRS source and not opened by me
"Usually ~90 days after Dec 31" for the run-out deadline: hedged with "usually" but unverified, and it varies by plan
"confirm the office will charge before the 15th": implies the charge date matters, when expenses count on the date of service (minor imprecision)
"spending $1,500 on stuff you wouldn't otherwise buy to save $680": an illustrative figure that does not match the user's numbers and is confusing
Cites a themjcos.com summary and the Rev. Proc. 2025-32 PDF: checkable links, not opened by me

reasons: Both answers correct the false premise in their opening lines, say a plan has one feature or neither, tell the person to call HR, and neither says the whole $1,900 is certainly lost. Neither mentions electing 2027 FSA money at open enrollment. B is cleaner on the figures: it gives the $680 maximum with a note that the plan may allow less, says "$1,220+" is lost on a carryover plan, covers the March 15, 2027 grace limit, and states plainly that run-out is for filing 2026 claims, not for new services. B's eligible-spend list is also broader. A is more concise and is the only one that clearly warns against prepaying for March work and pushes December scheduling, a point B only partly covers. A muddles its figure with a "$1,220–$1,240" range that draws on the 2025 plan-year cap, and its eligible list is thinner. The two are close; B gets a slight edge on correctness and completeness, and A's prepay warning keeps the gap small.
